rv.q: It is funny, witty and painfully aware — easily one of Rebeck's best works.
Rickman gives the comic performance of the season.
A slender but enjoyable play about the courage and self-knowledge required of any artist, with an ace ensemble led by Alan Rickman in fine form.
Alan Rickman is heaven-sent as the sexy, sneering, snarling literary legend who condescends to tutor four aspiring novelists who have paid through the nose for the privilege of being abused.
The play's saving grace is that it knows how to make us laugh.
But her plays aren't very good.
But it can’t sustain more than one thought or emotion or effect at the same time.

Maybe you can’t judge a book by its cover, but apparently you can come up with a spot-on appraisal just by eyeballing a couple of sentences. That, anyway, is the impression left by “Seminar,” the shiny, facile new comedy by Theresa Rebeck, which stars Alan Rickman as the posturing celebrity teacher of a writing workshop.

That’s a significant achievement, considering how intrinsically irritating all of these characters are and how vastly Rebeck’s interest in them outstrips our own, often by several orders of magnitude.
There are consolations, chief among them Rickman, who wisely understates Leonard's prickly intelligence, colossal ego, and enormous self-loathing.
Rickman and this extraordinary quartet, paced with feverish enthusiasm by Sam Gold, bring sexiness, verve and artistry to a tried-and-true formula.
Seminar is consistently clever and entertaining — and, under Sam Gold's briskly intelligent direction, a fine showcase for extraordinary actors.
That does add a touch of pleasing weight to a show that's as elaborately appointed as anything this feather-light can possibly be.
Leonard would have something barbed to say about him — and then approve.

cn.t: Critics find Rebeck's comedy thin and facile but elevated by Alan Rickman's delicious performance as a caustic writing teacher. The play starts funny but peters out, though Rickman's understated cruelty makes it watchable.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
